newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania opposition wary over Albania mission.
newsitem.headline: Romania opposition wary over Albania mission.

text.p: Romania's leftist opposition on Tuesday called into question the new centrist government's plans to send 400 Romanian troops on a multinational security mission in lawless Albania.

The Party of Social Democracy (PDSR) raised the doubts ahead of Thursday's vote in parliament on reformist President Emil Constantinescu's appeal for peacekeepers to be sent to Albania as part of a 6,000-strong Italian-led force.
Constantinescu is expected to have little difficulty winning the vote, despite the reservations.

The defence ministry said that once parliament gave its approval the first Romanian troops would be sent later this month to the Adriatic ports of Vlore and Sarande and the southern town of Gjirokaster -- all in rebel hands.

"Our troops will only be deployed in peaceful conditions," a ministry statement said, making deployment contingent on an accord between the command of the Italian-led force, Albanian authorities and the heads of rebel-run areas.

Teodor Melescanu, PDSR spokesman and a former foreign minister, said his party was unhappy with both the nature of the force and its vague brief under the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe.
"It is not a United Nations force, nor is it placed under the NATO flag, but under the flexible mandate of the OSCE," Melescanu said by telephone.
Other opposition objections ranged from the size of the planned Romanian contingent to the dangers of sending it to the heart of rebel-held southern Albania.
"Also, this force is being led by just one country, Italy, which I gather, is now facing problems itself," Melescanu said.

Italy's main centre-right opposition bloc supports the mission but said on Tuesday it would vote against a government resolution on the deployment of the force, scheduled for next week and taking in troops from NATO's southern flank, plus Romania.
"Rather than sending troops, we favour political intervention (in Albania)," Melescanu said.
Bucharest says its contribution to the Albania operation, due to stretch over six months, will cost about $9.5 million dollars, to be allotted from the government's budgetary reserves.
Romania has sent troops to the NATO-led IFOR mission in Bosnia as well on peacekeeping missions in Somalia and Angola.
Participation in the Albanian mission is clearly part of the government's drive to carve a role for Bucharest as a haven of stability in the volatile Balkans.
Pressing their longshot bid for early entry into NATO, the country's new leaders say their country could strengthen the southern flank of the Atlantic Alliance.

Bucharest is lobbying hard to be admitted alongside Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary when the alliance announces its first eastward expansion at a summit in Madrid in July. Western countries say its chances have improved since the centrists ousted ex-communists in last November's elections.
